strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining CLIP's semantic predictions with discriminative visual features for transductive zero-shot classification without updating pretrained network weights. Semantic initialization and iterative refinement provide an intuitive, practical mechanism.

The reported improvements are substantial and broad. Across 11 datasets, OTFusion improves average accuracy from 64.78% to 74.95% with CLIP ViT-B/16 and from 58.68% to 70.45% with ResNet-50, improving over CLIP on every dataset. Comparisons include relevant transductive methods such as TransCLIP and ECALP.

Table 2 provides useful component analysis. Visual features substantially improve over semantic-only transport, and joint refinement improves average accuracy from 71.67% to 74.95%. The sensitivity and iteration plots provide additional empirical evidence of stable behavior under the evaluated conditions.
weaknesses: The central joint-optimization claim is not technically established. Equations (4) and (6) maximize agreement with GMM posterior probabilities P, whereas the mean and covariance updates in Equations (11)–(12) optimize a Q-weighted Gaussian log-likelihood. These are different objectives, and no derivation connects the updates to ascent of the stated objective. Empirical stabilization in Figure 3 does not resolve this discrepancy. This affects the claimed optimization principle, beyond a presentation refinement.

The transport constraints are infeasible as written. Equation (5) requires all N row sums and all K column sums to equal one, implying total mass both N and K. For N unequal to K, no such Q exists. Equations (8)–(10) also reverse the scaling-vector dimensions relative to the N-by-K kernel. Although these may be correctable specification errors, the implemented marginals remain unclear. If uniform class mass is intended, its implications for imbalanced test distributions also need justification.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the contribution of the proposed fusion mechanism from the additional DINOv2 ViT-L/14 representation. In Table 2, DINOv2-only already reaches 74.20%, versus 74.95% for OTFusion, while feature concatenation reaches 75.54%. These results support the usefulness of visual features, but offer weaker support for the distinctive fusion contribution. There is no matched comparison applying competing transductive methods to the same visual resources, or a joint-refinement variant without transport balancing.

The claimed efficiency and scalability advantages are not measured. No runtime, peak-memory, or scaling results establish an advantage over concatenation or graph-based alternatives, despite these advantages being central to the motivation. Incorporating a large additional visual encoder has a meaningful cost, even without gradient updates.

Reproducibility and comparison consistency need improvement. Important details include the exact prompt, CLIP temperature, feature normalization, mixture-weight handling, covariance regularization, stopping criterion, and dataset split protocol. The stated diagonal covariance is inconsistent with the full-matrix expression in Equation (12). Table 1 and Table 2 also use different CLIP baseline results without explaining the difference.

Several reporting claims exceed the evidence. Table 1's ResNet-50 VisDesc and CALIP averages are listed as 61.76% and 64.00%, but their displayed entries average approximately 58.29% and 59.45%. The conclusion claims further gains with training-based adaptation methods, yet no such experiments are reported. These issues are individually correctable; the recommendation is primarily driven by the unresolved objective/update mismatch and insufficient isolation of the fusion contribution, despite the promising empirical gains.

strengths: The practical goal is useful: combine CLIP’s semantic predictions with DINOv2’s visual structure using unlabeled target images, without updating either backbone. Semantic initialization and iterative refinement provide an understandable mechanism for transferring class information into visual clusters.

The reported empirical gains are substantial and broad. Table 1 evaluates 11 datasets with two CLIP backbones, reporting average accuracies of 74.95% and 70.45%, versus 64.78% and 58.68% for CLIP. Improvements occur on every dataset, and the reported averages exceed strong transductive baselines such as TransCLIP and ECALP.

Table 2 provides useful component evidence: adding visual information substantially improves over semantic-only transport, and removing joint refinement reduces average accuracy from 74.95% to 71.67%. The sensitivity and iteration plots provide additional evidence of empirical stability.
weaknesses: The central optimization claim is not technically established. Equations (4) and (7) maximize a linear score involving GMM posterior probabilities P, whereas Equations (11)–(12) are weighted Gaussian maximum-likelihood updates. These updates do not generally maximize the stated posterior-score objective. No derivation or surrogate argument connects them, so the method is better supported as a heuristic alternating procedure than as joint optimization of the advertised objective. Figure 3 does not resolve this mismatch.

The transport problem is infeasible as written: Equation (5) requires every row and every column of an N-by-K matrix to sum to one, implying simultaneously total mass N and K. Equations (8)–(10) also reverse the required dimensions of the scaling vectors. Although these may be correctable notation errors, the actual marginals remain unspecified. A balanced correction would impose equal aggregate class mass, an assumption whose consequences for imbalanced target sets are not examined.

The experiments only partially isolate the contribution of the proposed fusion. OTFusion adds DINOv2 ViT-L/14 to comparisons primarily using CLIP, without evaluating competing transductive methods with equivalent visual features. In Table 2, the DINOv2-feature variant already achieves 74.20%, while feature concatenation reaches 75.54%, exceeding OTFusion’s 74.95%. This does not invalidate the method’s usefulness, but leaves its advantage over simpler feature integration unclear. There is also no direct comparison isolating Sinkhorn balancing from otherwise identical iterative probability fusion.

The claimed efficiency and scalability advantages are unsupported by runtime, peak-memory, or model-count scaling measurements. This matters because the method requires an additional large visual encoder and full-target-set iterative inference, and because scalability is its principal stated advantage over the stronger concatenation baseline. Claims that competing methods have higher computational costs are likewise not substantiated.

Reproducibility is limited by missing or inconsistent implementation details: the CLIP temperature, feature normalization, GMM mixture-weight handling, covariance regularization, and convergence criterion are not specified. The text describes a shared diagonal covariance, but Equation (12) produces a full covariance unless an unreported diagonal projection is applied. The exact multi-model configuration producing the main results and the unlabeled data splits used for adaptation also need clearer specification.

Several reporting issues weaken confidence, although they are not independently grounds for rejection. The CLIP baseline changes between Tables 1 and 2 without explanation. In Table 1(b), the listed VisDesc and CALIP dataset scores average approximately 58.29% and 59.45%, rather than the reported 61.76% and 64.00%. The conclusion claims additional gains when combined with training-based adaptation, but no corresponding experiments are presented. Overall, the promising empirical results do not yet outweigh the unresolved objective–algorithm mismatch and insufficient attribution of the proposed fusion’s benefit.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining CLIP's semantic predictions with DINOv2's visual structure without updating pretrained network weights. Semantic initialization and iterative refinement provide an understandable, potentially practical approach.

The reported improvements are substantial and broad. Across 11 datasets, Table 1 reports average accuracy gains from 64.78% to 74.95% with CLIP ViT-B/16 and from 58.68% to 70.45% with ResNet-50. Improvements occur on every evaluated dataset, with particularly large gains on EuroSAT and Flowers102.

Table 2 provides useful component evidence: CLIP-only visual modeling achieves 70.96%, DINOv2-only achieves 74.20%, and full fusion achieves 74.95%. Disabling joint refinement reduces accuracy to 71.67%, supporting the value of iterative interaction. Sensitivity and convergence plots provide additional empirical characterization.
weaknesses: The central optimization formulation is not technically consistent. Equation (5) requires an N-by-K matrix to have every row and column sum to one, implying total mass both N and K; the feasible set is empty when N differs from K. The scaling-vector dimensions in Equations (8)–(10) are also reversed. These may be correctable errors, but the actual implemented marginals are unspecified, and the implied uniform class-mass assumption is neither justified nor evaluated under class imbalance.

More substantively, the claimed alternating optimization is not derived from the stated objective. Equations (4) and (6) maximize linear agreement with normalized GMM posterior probabilities, whereas Equations (11)–(12) are weighted Gaussian maximum-likelihood updates. Those updates do not generally maximize the stated posterior-agreement objective. Empirical stabilization in Figure 3 does not establish that the algorithm optimizes this objective. This undermines the principal claim of a unified, principled joint optimization.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the benefit of the proposed transport fusion from access to stronger visual features. DINOv2-only already achieves 74.20%, while simple feature concatenation achieves 75.54%, exceeding OTFusion's 74.95%. A controlled comparison using the same CLIP and DINOv2 features with existing transductive methods, or a joint-refinement variant without transport constraints, is missing. Concatenation's stronger accuracy is not itself disqualifying, but the claimed compensating scalability advantage has no runtime or memory measurements.

Comparison reporting contains discrepancies that weaken confidence in the evaluation protocol. The CLIP baseline averages differ between Tables 1 and 2, with unexplained dataset-level differences. In Table 1(b), the listed VisDesc and CALIP results average approximately 58.29% and 59.45%, rather than the reported 61.76% and 64.00%. These arithmetic errors do not erase the reported gains, but require correction and clearer documentation of baseline sources and settings.

Reproducibility and practical claims are incompletely supported. The manuscript omits the CLIP temperature, precise prompt and feature normalization settings, mixture-weight handling, covariance regularization, and stopping tolerances; Equation (12) also specifies a full covariance despite the stated diagonal model. No timing or memory evidence supports the low-resource claims despite adding DINOv2 ViT-L/14. Claimed hybrid-method performance boosts and general fusion of multiple VLMs are not experimentally demonstrated. Overall, the promising empirical contribution is outweighed by the unresolved objective–algorithm mismatch and insufficient attribution of the fusion benefit, leading to weak rejection.

strengths: The framework addresses a useful problem: combining semantic predictions from VLMs with discriminative visual representations from VFMs without fine-tuning the foundation models. It supports both transductive prediction and inductive inference through fitted visual classifiers.

The evaluation spans natural images, remote sensing, and pathology, with substantial reported improvements. For example, CLIP+DINOv3 achieves 77.4% average transductive accuracy versus CLIP’s 65.2% in Table 1, and 77.2% versus 65.2% in the inductive setting.

Table 6 provides valuable ensemble comparisons beyond single-model baselines: SOTA achieves 81.45% on remote sensing and 83.90% on pathology, versus 77.46% and 78.07% for ensembles of ADAPT-adapted models. These results support practical value beyond simply adding models.

The ablations separate visual information, adaptive weighting, and joint refinement. Figure 4 supports the importance of joint refinement, while Table 5 demonstrates a larger benefit from adaptation when model quality differs substantially.
weaknesses: The central optimization guarantee is unsupported. The tangent minorization in Eq. (12) is valid, but its GMM-dependent term is a weighted sum of posterior probabilities. The GMM M-step in Eqs. (19)–(20) optimizes a different, complete-data log-likelihood objective and is not shown to increase this surrogate. Consequently, the claimed monotonic improvement and stationary-point convergence in Appendix 6.1 do not follow. Figure 5 plots accuracy rather than objective values and cannot validate this claim.

The transport constraints are both underspecified and inconsistently implemented in the equations. The manuscript never explains how the class marginal q is obtained, although this directly determines predicted class proportions and is essential to assessing the 'prior-free' claim. Eqs. (17)–(18) use all-ones targets, which have unequal total mass for a rectangular N-by-K transport matrix, and the stated scaling-vector dimensions are reversed. These issues prevent reproducing the stated solver and leave its behavior on imbalanced data unclear.

Several consequential implementation details are missing: initialization and semantic alignment of GMM components, the VLM temperature tau, mixture-weight updates, covariance regularization, and precise inductive training splits. Eq. (19) also contains an undefined Q, while Eq. (20) specifies a shared covariance and the complexity discussion assumes diagonal covariances. The abstract’s code-availability statement has no link, so the provided manuscript does not resolve these ambiguities.

The strongest natural-image comparisons confound algorithmic improvements with access to additional, stronger DINO-L representations. No competing method using the same CLIP+DINO features is reported. Moreover, Figure 4 attributes only 0.2, 0.3, and 0.8 percentage points to the headline adaptive mechanism, without variability estimates. The domain ensemble comparisons are useful, but the evidence for the specific weighting innovation is less compelling than the overall system gains.

Agreement with the current transport plan is treated as evidence of model reliability, although it can also reward confidently incorrect predictions or correlated errors. Table 5 provides some empirical support, but calibration sensitivity and robustness to misleading models remain unexamined. Overall, the promising empirical contribution is outweighed by the unresolved objective–update mismatch and insufficient specification of the actual algorithm, leading to a weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The problem is useful: combining semantically aligned VLM predictions with stronger visual representations could improve zero-shot classification without updating foundation-model weights. The framework supports both transductive prediction and inductive classifiers.

The empirical gains are substantial and span natural images, remote sensing, and pathology. Table 1 reports 77.8% average accuracy for CLIP with DINOv2/v3 versus 65.2% for CLIP, while Tables 2–3 report 81.5% and 83.9% for the domain-specific ensembles.

The supplement includes meaningful ensemble comparisons rather than only individual-model baselines. Table 6 reports improvements over mean ensembling and ensembles of adapted models, including ADAPT: 81.45% versus 77.46% for remote sensing and 83.9% versus 78.07% for pathology.

The fixed-posterior transport update has a valid tangent-minorization motivation. Ablations distinguish visual information, adaptive weighting, and coupled learning; the reported benefits of coupling are appreciable.
weaknesses: The central joint-optimization guarantee is unsupported. Equation (12) requires improving a weighted sum of posterior probabilities with respect to GMM parameters. The ordinary soft-assignment GMM M-step in Equations (19)–(20) instead optimizes an expected complete-data log likelihood; it is not shown to increase that surrogate. Therefore, the valid minorization of the squared terms does not establish monotonicity or stationary-point convergence of the full algorithm, as claimed in Section 6.1. Figure 5 tracks accuracy, not the objective, and cannot resolve this issue.

The transport constraints are insufficiently specified and the stated solver is inconsistent. The method requires sample and class marginals p and q, but their experimental construction is not explained, leaving the 'prior-free' claim unsubstantiated. Equations (16)–(18) reuse these symbols as scaling vectors, reverse their dimensions relative to the N-by-K kernel, and use all-ones targets whose total masses differ when N differs from K. This obscures the actual class-balance assumption and prevents faithful implementation of a central component.

Additional implementation omissions materially limit reproducibility. The manuscript does not specify semantic initialization of the GMM components and transport plan, the VLM temperature, mixture-weight updates, or covariance regularization. Equation (19) contains an undefined Q, while Equation (20) displays a shared full covariance but Section 8.3 analyzes diagonal covariances. Initialization is particularly consequential because independently fitted mixture components have no inherent correspondence to class names. The abstract's code-availability statement supplies no URL.

The evidence only partially isolates the proposed adaptive mechanism. Figure 4 reports gains of 0.2, 0.3, and 0.8 percentage points over fixed weighting, without variability estimates; Table 5 provides stronger but still limited supporting evidence. The largest natural-image gains also introduce large DINO encoders without corresponding baselines using the same representations. Thus, those comparisons establish the usefulness of additional visual features more clearly than the advantage of the particular fusion objective.

Agreement with the current transport plan is treated as model reliability without adequately testing calibration or confirmation bias. The weights in Equation (13) can reward confident predictions that agree with an already incorrect plan. Model-subset experiments are helpful, but do not establish the claimed robustness to noisy distributions. Overall, the broad empirical merits are worthwhile, yet the unresolved objective–algorithm mismatch and incomplete transport specification currently outweigh them.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining semantic predictions from vision-language models with discriminative visual representations, without fine-tuning foundation-model weights. Supporting both transductive prediction and inductive classifiers increases its practical relevance.

The reported empirical gains are substantial across three domains. Table 1 improves average natural-image accuracy from 65.2% for CLIP to 77.8% using CLIP and two DINO models; Tables 2–3 report 81.5% on remote sensing and 83.9% on pathology.

The supplementary ensemble comparisons strengthen the evidence beyond comparisons with individual models. Table 6 reports improvements over ensembles of adapted models, including 81.45% versus 77.46% for ADAPT on remote sensing and 83.9% versus 78.07% on pathology.

The ablations provide useful evidence for incorporating visual distributions and jointly refining assignments and GMM parameters. Model-subset experiments and computational measurements further support the framework’s potential usefulness.
weaknesses: The central optimization guarantee is unsupported. The tangent minorization of squared agreement is valid, but the GMM M-step in Eqs. (19)–(20) optimizes a weighted Gaussian complete-data log-likelihood, whereas the surrogate in Eq. (12) contains posterior probabilities directly. These are different objectives, and the manuscript does not establish that the GMM update increases the surrogate. Consequently, the claimed monotonic improvement and stationary-point convergence of the full algorithm do not follow. Figure 5 plots accuracy, which cannot verify objective convergence.

The transport constraints are insufficiently specified and conflict with the implementation equations. The method requires sample and class marginals p and q, but their actual selection or estimation is not explained, leaving the 'prior-free' claim unsubstantiated. Eqs. (16)–(18) reuse these symbols for scaling vectors, reverse their stated dimensions, and use all-ones target marginals whose total masses differ when N and K differ. This prevents literal reproduction of the central transport step and leaves its class-balance assumptions unclear.

Other missing implementation details materially affect reproducibility: initialization of the transport plan and semantically indexed GMM components, the VLM temperature, mixture-weight updates, and covariance regularization are unspecified. Eq. (19) introduces an undefined Q, while Eq. (20) gives a shared covariance expression and the complexity discussion assumes diagonal covariances. The inductive training splits and exact final prediction rule also need specification.

Attribution of gains to the headline adaptive mechanism remains limited. Figure 4 reports only 0.2, 0.3, and 0.8 percentage-point gains over fixed weighting, without variability estimates; Table 5 provides stronger but still modest evidence. Natural-image comparisons also introduce large DINO encoders absent from most baselines, so they do not isolate the proposed fusion rule from improved representations. Agreement with the current transport plan is not independently established as a reliable measure of model quality.

Some presentation claims overstate the results. Section 4.1 claims an approximately 6.9-point advantage over the best competitor, whereas Table 1 gives 77.4% versus 74.5% for CLIP+DINOv3, a 2.9-point difference. These reporting issues are secondary; the recommendation is driven by the unresolved objective–algorithm mismatch and underspecified transport procedure, which outweigh the otherwise promising empirical contribution.
